newsitem.title: USA: USDA nears deadline for FY97 sugar import quota.
newsitem.headline: USDA nears deadline for FY97 sugar import quota.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department neared its deadline for setting the fiscal 1997 sugar import quota on Thursday and it appeared the quota would have to be reduced from the proposed 2.475 million tonnes.
USDA has said it would announce its decision by Friday. At mid-week, all signs pointed to the deadline being met.
Along with setting the quota, USDA has proposed adoption of a formula to review the quota level three times a year.
Based on figures in the latest World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates report, sugar imports might be held to a level 200,000 tonnes below the maximum proposed by USDA.

The report boosted U.S. sugar production to an estimated 7.05 million short tons, which would mean a total supply of 11.629 million tons if the full 2.727 million tons of imports were allowed. Use was reduced to 10.025 million tons.
Together, the figures suggest ending stocks of 1.604 million tons and a stocks to use ratio of 16 percent.
Along with the quota, USDA proposed a formula for adjusting the import quota with the balance point being a stocks ratio of 15.5 percent.

Under USDA'S proposed formula, the import quota would be reduced by 200,000 tonnes, or 220,460 short tons, if USDA's projected stocks ratio exceeded 15.5 percent in November, February and May. If it was below 15.5 percent, the 200,000 tonne increment would be allocated among quota-holding nations.

Sugar users have urged USDA to use a high stocks ratio, as high as 20 percent, as the trigger. Growers have argued for a lower trigger level, perhaps 13 or 14 percent, on grounds they otherwise would be hit by unfairly low prices.
